editorNote: Home-computer games, optical-disc ambitions and the cost of going online fill the late-summer desk.
morningLine: Four elements, four Adepts—and a reserve of magic that will not last forever.

lead.headline: Archon II: Adept makes every spell count
lead.dek: Free Fall’s fantasy contest trades familiar territory for an elemental struggle over energy.
body: Archon II: Adept brings the meeting of strategy and arcade combat back to the home computer, but not as a simple second helping of the original board. Arthur Leyenberger’s review in the August COMPUTE! describes a contest built around magical energy and the four elements. Electronic Arts publishes the Free Fall Associates game.

Each side begins with four Adepts, positioned on Earth, Water, Air and Fire. Moving across the strategic board is only half the business: opposing pieces settle their encounters in individual real-time combat. The player must consider both position and the ability to win the next fight.

Spells and powerful creatures draw down the energy reserve. Power points offer replenishment, making the struggle for territory a struggle for resources as well. Beginner and advanced settings alter starting energy and combat speed, allowing opponents of different experience to meet on more useful terms.

The Apocalypse spell can force a final one-on-one battle shaped by surviving pieces and resources. The August review lists Commodore 64 or 128, Atari 400/800 or XL with at least 48K, and Apple II-series machines with at least 48K; a disk drive and joystick are required. The Apple edition is listed at $40. This is the month’s review desk, not a claim of a new release this week.

stories.headline: Atari puts an encyclopedia on an optical disc
stories.dek: A 520ST demonstration points beyond the floppy disk.
body: An encyclopedia can occupy a shelf—or, in Atari’s working demonstration described in the August COMPUTE!, a fraction of an optical disc. Tom R. Halfhill’s Summer CES report describes a prototype connected to a 520ST, with Activenture software providing the indexing.

The demonstration holds a 23-volume, nine-million-word encyclopedia plus index while leaving three-quarters of the disc empty. Entries can be retrieved within seconds. Activenture’s Tom Rolander sees legal and medical reference works, cookbooks and other large databases as possible applications, not products already on sale.

Atari hopes for availability late in 1985 or early in 1986 at about $500. Those remain plans reported from the show. The encyclopedia publisher is unnamed because a final contract has not been signed.

stories.headline: WordPerfect makes a blank screen its selling point
stories.dek: The writing surface stays clean while the machinery waits behind it.
body: Richard Mansfield’s August COMPUTE! review makes a case for WordPerfect’s unobtrusive writing screen. Persistent control codes and command lines do not crowd the text; a separate control-code screen can be called up when the writer needs it.

A 100,000-word expandable spelling dictionary includes phonetic lookup, and the review describes detection of repeated words. Macros, two editing screens, automatic backup saving, footnotes, calculations, outline numbering and tables of contents widen the assignment beyond simple typing.

The listed price is $495 from SSI Software of Orem, Utah. The review calls for an IBM PC or compatible with 192K RAM, two disk drives, DOS 2.0 or later and a printer, and explicitly excludes the PCjr. No version number is assigned here beyond the review’s own identification.

stories.headline: Behind the SIG, an online business
stories.dek: File libraries and conferences take more than a modem to keep running.
body: Arlon R. Levitan’s August COMPUTE! column looks behind commercial special-interest groups. Topic-based messages, downloadable files and live conferences form the three principal attractions, with operators competing to keep members returning.

Levitan reports that leading SIGs generate well over $1 million annually and that some head sysops or sponsoring companies receive at least five percent of gross. Assistant sysops commonly receive free SIG time rather than wages, according to the column. These are the columnist’s estimates, not audited accounts.

Delphi and The Source are described as challengers to CompuServe. For the household caller, reading downloaded messages and preparing replies offline can keep the hourly meter from running while the thinking is done.

market.headline: The telephone meter joins the hardware bill
market.summary: August Antic lists CompuServe night access at $6 an hour for 300 baud and $7.75 for 1200. Faster hardware and service tariffs both belong in the home-computing budget; these are printed August rates, not a new price announcement.

worldAnchor.headline: Discovery lifts off with communications satellites
worldAnchor.summary: Discovery launches on STS-51I on August 27 at 6:58 a.m. EDT, carrying ASC-1, AUSSAT-1 and SYNCOM IV-4. Joe Engle commands the five-person crew.

bbsNote.headline: Atari users weigh modem speed against the hourly meter
bbsNote.summary: Michael Ciraolo’s Antic August 1985 guide supplies specific modem/interface prices, online rates and community expansion; Levitan’s August COMPUTE! column explains SIG economics. Notes below are editorial summaries of printed reporting, not fabricated BBS messages.

posts.text: Antic lists night access at $6/hour for 300 baud and $7.75/hour for 1200; regular entry fee $40, often discounted or waived. ANTIC ONLINE and SIG*Atari are identified as community destinations.

posts.topic: A second home for Atari communities
posts.text: Antic reports planned duplication of SIG*ATARI files and ANTIC ONLINE on Delphi; $50 lifetime registration includes two evening hours; $6/hour evenings at either 300 or 1200 baud, $16 daytime, no monthly minimum.

The Source: $100 regular registration, $7.75/hour evenings/weekends and $10 monthly minimum. Dow Jones: $72/hour day, $12/hour night. Attribute all rates to Antic August 1985; no claim of this week’s price changes.
Levitan reports large SIGs generating over $1 million a year and some lead operators receiving at least five percent of gross, with volunteer assistants compensated by free time.

curiosity.headline: Your Mickey Mouse telephone may not fit your modem
curiosity.summary: Antic’s introductory modem guide finds a surprisingly practical obstacle in novelty-shaped handsets.
curiosity.detail: Michael Ciraolo explains that acoustic-coupler modems use rubber cups to hold the telephone handset and specifically notes that unusual shapes such as Mickey Mouse phones will not work. This is a sourced August 1985 observation, not a newly announced peripheral.

undergroundDesk.headline: 2600 challenges the seizure of Private Sector
undergroundDesk.dek: August commentary disputes the treatment of a bulletin-board community.
body: The August issue of 2600 reports that New Jersey authorities seized the Private Sector BBS on July 12 and charged its operator on July 18. These are July events being covered in an August publication, not a raid during this issue’s week.

The magazine disputes guilt by association and sensational satellite-hacking claims, and says the ACLU has taken up the defense. As a publication involved in the scene, its account is an interested source: its allegations and arguments are not judicial findings. The episode puts the status of a board and its users at the center of the argument.
